question: What does the Doppler principle allow a system to measure?

options.text: The distance between transmitter and receiver
The height of the transmitter above the receiver
The bearing of the transmitter from the receiver
Relative speed between transmitter and receiver

explanation: Any relative motion between transmitter and receiver shifts the received frequency. Measuring the difference between transmitted and received frequency gives the relative speed — the basis of police speed radar and Doppler navigation.

question: When is the received frequency exactly the same as the transmitted frequency?

options.text: Only when there is no relative motion between them
Only when the receiver is directly below the transmitter
Whenever the transmitter is more powerful than the receiver
Only when both are moving in the same direction

explanation: Any closing or opening speed between transmitter and receiver produces a Doppler shift. With no relative motion — even if both move at the same velocity together — the frequencies match.

question: A receiver and transmitter are moving towards each other. How does the received frequency compare with the transmitted one?

options.text: It is higher only if the transmitter moves
It is the same
It is higher
It is lower

explanation: Closing motion crowds the wavefronts together, so more cycles arrive per second and the received frequency rises. Moving apart lowers it.

question: A transmitter moves away from a stationary receiver. What happens to the received frequency?

options.text: It stays the same, because the receiver is stationary
It decreases, in proportion to the speed
It increases, in proportion to the speed
It decreases, in proportion to the distance

explanation: Opening motion stretches the spacing between wavefronts, so fewer cycles arrive per second. The shift depends on the relative speed, not on the distance.

question: What is the Doppler shift?

options.text: The change in polarization on reflection
The change in signal strength caused by the relative speed
Received minus transmitted frequency
The time delay between transmitting and receiving

explanation: The Doppler shift (Doppler frequency) is the difference between the frequency received and the frequency transmitted. It is proportional to the relative speed.

question: How does the Doppler shift change if the closing speed doubles?

options.text: It quadruples
It doubles
It halves
It does not change

explanation: Doppler shift is directly proportional to the relative speed: twice the speed, twice the shift.

question: For an echo from a surface, the Doppler shift is approximately 2V/λ. Why the factor of 2?

options.text: The signal is shifted going out and again coming back
The speed of radio waves is halved on reflection
The frequency is doubled by reflection from the ground
The aircraft has two aerials, one for each direction

explanation: In a radar, the moving aircraft both transmits and receives. The frequency is shifted on the path to the surface and again on the path back, so the total shift is twice the one-way value.

question: A Doppler radar on 10 GHz (λ = 3 cm) is closing on the ground at 150 m/s along its beam. What is the Doppler shift (Δf ≈ 2V/λ)?

options.text: 4.5 kHz
20 kHz
5 kHz
10 kHz

explanation: Δf = 2 × 150 / 0.03 = 300 / 0.03 = 10 000 Hz = 10 kHz. Leaving out the factor of 2 gives 5 kHz.

question: Which of these systems make use of the Doppler principle?

options.text: Radio altimeter, NDB and ADF
ILS localizer, ILS glide path and DME
Radar, Doppler VOR and VDF
NDB, marker beacons and DME

explanation: Besides Doppler navigation, the principle is used in radar (moving target and weather velocity processing), in Doppler VOR and in some VDF systems.

question: Standing still in the sea, waves reach you four times a minute. You walk towards the waves. What do you notice?

options.text: They reach you more often because they are produced faster
They reach you more often, though they are produced at the same rate
They reach you at the same rate as before
They reach you less often, because you are moving

explanation: Moving towards the source shortens the time between wave arrivals, so the perceived frequency rises. The source's own frequency has not changed — this is the Doppler effect.

question: Who first predicted the Doppler effect, and for what kind of waves?

options.text: Christian Doppler, for radio waves
Heinrich Hertz, for sound waves
Guglielmo Marconi, for radio waves
Christian Doppler, for light waves

explanation: The Austrian physicist Christian Doppler predicted it in the 19th century in connection with light. It applies equally to sound and radio waves.

question: What does an airborne Doppler navigation system measure directly?

options.text: Ground speed and drift
Wind velocity and track
Position and altitude
True airspeed and heading

explanation: Doppler measures the aircraft's motion over the ground: its speed along track (ground speed) and across track (giving drift). Heading must come from elsewhere to work out position.

question: What kind of aerial does a typical airborne Doppler use?

options.text: One slotted waveguide array for transmit and receive
A rotating parabolic dish in the nose radome
A loop and sense aerial on top of the fuselage
Separate blade aerials for each of its beams on the belly

explanation: A slotted waveguide antenna pointing downwards sends an array of beams to the ground. Transmitter and receiver elements share it but are screened from each other.

question: What is a Janus array?

options.text: An arrangement of beams all pointing straight down
Beams pointing both forwards and aft
A pair of beams pointing left and right only
Two aerials, one on top of the fuselage and one below

explanation: Named after the Roman god of doorways who faced both ways, a Janus array uses beams angled forwards and backwards — commonly four, sometimes three.

question: How many beams does a Janus array normally use?

options.text: Exactly two
Six or eight
One or two
Three or four

explanation: Janus arrays normally use 3 or 4 beams; the 4-beam layout (two forward, two aft) is the common one.

question: An aircraft flies straight ahead with no drift. What do the four Janus beams detect?

options.text: A shift in the left beams only, opposite to the right beams
No shift in any beam, because there is no drift
Equal, opposite shifts: up forward, down aft
Equal shifts upwards in all four beams, proportional to speed

explanation: The forward beams are closing on the ground (frequency increase) and the aft beams opening (decrease). With no drift the left and right pairs agree, and the size of the shift gives the ground speed.

question: What tells a Doppler system that the aircraft is drifting?

options.text: A loss of signal in one of the aft beams
Unequal port and starboard beam shifts
An increase in the shift in all four beams together
A difference between the forward and aft beam shifts

explanation: Sideways movement over the ground makes the left and right beams see different shifts. Processing that difference gives the drift; the fore-aft shift gives the ground speed.

question: In older Doppler systems with a moving aerial, how was drift measured?

options.text: The aerial was locked to the fuselage and drift came from the aft beams alone
The aerial was pointed at a ground station and drift came from the bearing
The aerial was turned to equalise port and starboard shifts; its angle gave drift
The pilot turned the aircraft until the shifts were equal and read the heading change

explanation: A motor drove the pitch-stabilized aerial until its beams lay along the track (equal port and starboard shifts). A pick-off measured the angle between that and the fore-aft axis — the drift.

question: What extra input does a Doppler navigation computer need to calculate position?

options.text: The bearing of a ground station
The aircraft's pressure altitude
The aircraft's true airspeed
The aircraft's heading

explanation: Doppler gives ground speed and drift. With a heading reference and a known starting position, the computer works out the position by dead reckoning, displayed as latitude and longitude or as along- and across-track distances.

question: Which problems of early Doppler systems are reduced by combining Doppler with IRS, VOR/DME or GPS?

options.text: Poor heading input and lost returns over water
Errors caused by the aircraft's altitude
Excess weight, bulk and high electrical power consumption
Interference from sky waves at night

explanation: Early systems suffered from inaccurate heading inputs and from weak or lost returns over large expanses of water. Blending in other sensors overcomes both.

question: Why can a Doppler navigation system lose accuracy over a calm sea?

options.text: A smooth sea reflects the beams away from the aircraft
Sea water absorbs SHF energy completely
The sea reverses the circular polarization of the beams
The sea surface moves, adding a false ground speed

explanation: A calm sea acts like a mirror and reflects the angled beams forward, away from the aircraft, so the returns are weak or lost. A moving sea surface can also add small errors.

question: In which direction are the beams of an airborne Doppler aimed?

options.text: Upwards, towards navigation satellites
Downwards towards the ground, angled forward and aft
Straight ahead, like a weather radar
Sideways, at right angles to the fuselage

explanation: The beams are directed down to the earth's surface, angled forwards and backwards (and to each side), so the ground return shows the aircraft's motion over the ground.

question: How did early Doppler navigation computers display the aircraft's position?

options.text: As a radial and DME distance from a VOR
As a grid reference on a moving map only
As latitude and longitude, or along- and across-track distance
As a relative bearing to the nearest NDB

explanation: The computer combined ground speed, drift and heading from a known departure point and showed the position as latitude/longitude or as NM along and across track.

question: Which beams detect a fall in received frequency when an aircraft is flying forwards?

options.text: The port beams only
The forward-pointing beams
None; all beams show a rise
The aft-pointing beams

explanation: The aft beams are moving away from the ground they illuminate, so their echoes are shifted down in frequency, while the forward beams see an increase.

question: Why are modern Doppler systems usually combined with IRS, VOR/DME or GPS?

options.text: To overcome heading errors and loss of returns over water
Because Doppler cannot measure ground speed
Because Doppler works only on the ground
To provide the radar returns for weather

explanation: Doppler gives accurate velocity, but early systems suffered from poor heading inputs and weak returns over smooth sea. Blending with other sensors fixes both.
